Preparing for solar or battery storage at your business?

Start with the information that makes an energy assessment useful:
• Recent electricity bills or prepaid records
• Monthly consumption and electricity spend
• Operating days and hours
• Site location and available space
• Existing solar, batteries or generators
• Your main priority: costs, backup, expansion or a combination

You do not need a finished technical brief. Start with what you have, and Ziya Energy will help identify what needs to be assessed next.

Solar panels and backup power do different jobs.

☀️ Solar panels generate electricity from sunlight.
🔋 Batteries store energy for later use.

A conventional grid-tied solar system may shut down during a grid outage—even when the sun is shining. Backup needs the right inverter, controls, wiring and system design.

Before choosing equipment, define the job:
• Which loads must stay on?
• How much power do they need at once?
• For how long?
• When does your business use the most energy?

Start with those answers, then size the system around your operating profile.

What still needs power at your business after sunset?

Your monthly electricity bill is a starting point. A night-load list helps explain where the energy is needed.

Swipe for the checklist, then record:
1. The equipment and its running power.
2. When it operates and for how long.
3. Which loads run at the same time.

Refrigeration, security and essential lighting are examples—not a ready-made list for every site. Motors may also need extra power to start, and cycling equipment does not necessarily draw its rated power all night.

Battery energy capacity (kWh) and the power needed at one time (kW) answer different questions. Usable capacity, losses, controls and the charging plan also matter. Measured load data helps turn the list into a suitable design.

Before accepting a solar quote, ask these three questions.

1. What is included?
Ask for the equipment, installation, electrical protection, commissioning and any backup circuits to be listed in writing. Check warranty and after-sales responsibilities too.

2. What costs extra?
Confirm VAT, exclusions, additional electrical work and any recurring charges. Compare complete scopes—not just the headline total.

3. What supports the savings estimate?
Ask which load profile, tariff, solar-production assumptions and operating strategy were used. Expected savings need a calculation, and actual results depend on the site and system.
